In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the total radiation dose has a significant impact on survival in palliative thoracic radiation for patients with advanced lung cancer.
the impact of total radiation dose on survival in lung cancer patients receiving palliative thoracic radiation therapy.
the question of whether higher total radiation doses in palliative thoracic irradiation of patients with lung cancer are associated with better survival.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
higher doses of palliative thoracic radiation do not improve survival in most patients, but may be considered in selected patients with good performance status and limited extrathoracic metastases.
higher EQD2 may have a small but not significant effect on 2-year survival.
higher doses of radiotherapy are probably not superior to lower doses with regard to 1- and/or 2-year survival.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
palliative radiotherapy for lung cancer patients should be given with the intent to deliver at least 30 Gy in 2-GY fractions.
palliative thoracic irradiation should be prescribed with the highest biologically equivalent doses that are feasible.
the use of higher EQD2 doses is not recommended for patients with poor performance status and/or extrathoracic progression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the survival benefit of higher dose radiotherapy for palliative treatment of lung cancer is small.
higher radiation dose is associated with longer survival in patients who receive radiotherapy as a palliative treatment for non-small cell lung carcinoma.
higher doses of radiation may improve survival in patients with good performance status and without extrathoracic progression.
